plain: Money is willing to chase returns and favors offensive sectors such as tech and consumer discretionary; the market mood is upbeat.
example: Over the last 20 trading days tech and discretionary stocks rose more than utilities and staples, which looks like risk-on.
notMeans: It does not mean prices will keep rising, and it is not a signal to buy.

plain: Money does not clearly favor offense or defense; everyone is waiting for a direction.
example: Offensive and defensive sectors rise by similar amounts and volatility is low.
notMeans: Neutral does not mean the market will stay flat; it can turn at any time.

plain: Money prefers steadier places such as utilities, staples and cash; the market mood is cautious.
example: Stocks fall while short-term Treasuries do better than stocks over the same period.
notMeans: It does not mean a crash is imminent, nor that the bottom is in.

plain: Sums up the last 20 trading days of money flow into risk-on, neutral or risk-off, with a probability for each.
example: Risk-on 90%, neutral 1%, risk-off 9%: today looks most like risk-on.
notMeans: The probability is how well today matches a historical state, not the chance that prices rise.

plain: A 0–100 mood thermometer: lower is more fearful, higher is greedier. It combines several public market gauges.
example: A reading of 43 falls in the fear band (25–44).
notMeans: Extreme fear is not always a bottom and extreme greed is not always a top.

plain: Measures how much volatility the market expects in US stocks over the next 30 days. The higher it is, the more nervous people are.
example: It usually sits between 12 and 20 and jumps on big events.
notMeans: A high reading does not mean a fall is coming, only that big swings are expected.

plain: How much a price swings up and down. High volatility means sharper moves in both directions.
example: 16% annualized volatility: over a year the price typically swings around 16% either way.
notMeans: High volatility does not mean falling; rallies can be sharp too.

plain: A common unit for interest rates. 1 bp = 0.01%, 100 bp = 1%.
example: A rate moving from 4.78% to 5.31% rose 53 bp.

plain: The rate the US government pays to borrow for 10 years; it works as a benchmark price of money. When it is high, borrowing is costly and stock valuations tend to be pressed down.
example: When yields rise, growth companies (whose profits lie far in the future) are usually hit harder.
notMeans: It is not simply 'yields up, stocks down'; the reason for the move matters.

plain: The 10-year rate minus the 2-year rate. Normally long rates are higher, so the spread is positive.
example: 0.47% means the 10-year rate is 0.47 percentage points above the 2-year rate.

plain: Short-term rates are higher than long-term rates, so the spread is negative. It has often appeared before slowdowns, so markets watch it closely.
example: A 2-year rate of 4.9% and a 10-year rate of 4.5% give a spread of −0.4%: inverted.
notMeans: Inversion is not a sure sign of recession and the timing is hard to predict.

plain: Offensive sectors (tech, discretionary, industrials) tend to gain most when the economy is good; defensive sectors (utilities, staples, health care) are needed even when it is weak.
example: In good times people buy new phones and travel (offense); in bad times they still need power, groceries and care (defense).
notMeans: This is a common grouping; individual companies may not fit.

plain: A sector's (or stock's) return minus the market's return. Above 0 means it beat the market.
example: Tech rose 5% and the market rose 3%, so relative strength is +2%.
notMeans: Beating the market does not mean it will keep doing so; sector leadership rotates.

plain: A statistical method that lets a computer find the typical 'states' in historical data on its own, instead of using hand-written rules.
example: Shown five series of history, it separates three common combinations by itself.
notMeans: It is not a crystal ball; it only works out which past situation today resembles.

plain: The stocks that make up an index. The index moves as these stocks move together, weighted.
example: The S&P 500's constituents are 500 large US companies.

plain: An index of 500 large US companies, often used to represent the US stock market.
example: Apple, Microsoft and Amazon are in it.

plain: The 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq, with a high share of tech stocks.
An index of 300 large, actively traded companies in the A-share market.
An index of the most representative large companies in the Hong Kong market.
How the company itself is doing: is it expensive, is it growing, does it make money. This is separate from recent price moves.
example: A company with steadily growing sales and profit that ranks well among peers has good fundamentals.
notMeans: Good fundamentals do not mean the price will rise; it may already be expensive or out of favor for now.

plain: Each of five items (valuation, growth, profitability, momentum, earnings-estimate revisions) is scored, averaged and mapped to a letter. The higher the letter, the more it leads its industry.
example: A+ means it ranks in roughly the top 7% of its industry (93 points or more).
notMeans: The grade describes the present; it is not a recommendation and does not predict returns.

plain: Where you rank in a group. The 80th percentile means higher than 80% of peers.
example: A profitability score of 85 means stronger than 85% of companies in the industry.
notMeans: A percentile only shows rank, not absolute level; if the whole industry is weak, being first may still be weak.

plain: A group of companies doing similar business. Comparisons are made within an industry so that, say, banks are not compared directly with tech firms.
example: US stocks use the 11 GICS sectors, A-shares use Shenwan level 1 and Hong Kong uses Hang Seng level 1.

plain: Whether the current price is expensive relative to what the company earns, often measured by the P/E ratio.
example: Of two companies with the same profit, the one with the higher price has the higher valuation (is pricier).
notMeans: A low valuation does not mean the price will rise; sometimes cheap has a reason.

plain: Price divided by annual earnings per share. Roughly: how many years of current profit it takes to earn back the price.
example: A P/E of 20 means the price is 20 times one year of profit.
notMeans: There is no absolute good or bad level; compare with the industry and its own history.

plain: How fast the company's sales and profit are growing.
example: Sales growing 20% a year is faster growth than 3% a year.
notMeans: Fast growth may not last, and may already be in the price.

plain: How efficiently the company makes money, e.g. how much profit is left from every 100 of sales.
example: A 25% margin leaves 25 of profit on every 100 sold.

plain: The tendency of recent price moves: if it has risen a lot lately, momentum is strong.
example: Gains over the last 3, 6 and 12 months all rank near the top of peers: strong momentum.
notMeans: Strong momentum does not mean it will keep rising; it may just be overheated.

plain: The profit a company makes in a year divided across each share.
example: A company earning 1 billion with 500 million shares has EPS of 2.

plain: Whether analysts raise or lower their forecasts for a company's future profit.
example: If several analysts lift this year's EPS forecast from 5.0 to 5.5, that is an upward revision.
notMeans: An upward revision does not guarantee a rising price; the market may have priced it in.

plain: An analyst's view of a stock (such as buy, hold, sell). An upgrade or downgrade means the view improved or worsened.
example: A move from hold to buy is an upgrade.
notMeans: Analysts can be wrong; a rating change is not a trade recommendation.

plain: A position marker that Chan theory identifies from the shape of the price path (strokes, pivots), including type 1–3 buy and sell points. It describes the move; it is not a trade order.
example: A 'type-1 buy' says: in a downtrend this leg has less force than the previous one.
notMeans: It does not predict returns and is not advice.

plain: A signal that appears while the last stroke is still running; under Chan rules it does not count until that stroke finishes.
example: The grey dashed badges on the chart are pending signals.
notMeans: A pending signal can disappear and is not an established buy or sell point.

plain: The day a buy or sell point is truly confirmed, a few days after the price turn.
example: Price bottoms on Sept 22 but is only confirmed on Sept 30; the confirmation date is Sept 30.

plain: How much of your total money you put into one stock, as a share.
example: Putting 20k of 100k into one stock is a 20% position.
notMeans: There is no standard answer; it depends on how much loss you can bear.

plain: How far a price has fallen from its peak.
example: From 100 down to 80 is a 20% drawdown.
notMeans: A small drawdown so far does not mean a large one cannot happen.

plain: Past prices are adjusted for dividends and splits so before and after can be compared, avoiding fake gaps on ex-dates.
example: After a 2-for-1 split the price halves overnight; an unadjusted chart would show a fake crash.

plain: The set of rules that decides what counts as a buy or sell point. Strict gives the fewest and follows the Chan textbook; Balanced (default) also counts divergence inside ranges, about twice as many; Relaxed gives the most and the earliest, even marking the last unfinished stroke.
example: For the same stock, Strict may show a single 1st buy on the chart while Relaxed shows several more.
notMeans: A looser rule is not more accurate; it just shows more signals, and they are easier to overturn.

plain: The average closing price of the last N candles, drawn as a line to show the rough direction of price over that stretch. Shorter lines (e.g. 5) hug the current price; longer ones (e.g. 60) are smoother and slower. Daily and 30-minute charts use 5 / 20 / 60; weekly uses 5 / 10 / 20.
example: A 20-day average of 10 means the average close over the last 20 trading days is about 10; a price above it is higher than that period's average.
notMeans: It is only an average of past prices and predicts nothing; price above or below the line does not mean it will keep rising or falling, and it is not a buy or sell signal.
